1 · Read the explanation.
Describing figures without reading them out

A table is precise and unreadable. A sentence about a table is imprecise and useful. The job of a quantifier here is to tell the listener the shape of the number: is it nearly everybody, about half, or almost nobody?

Two decisions come first. Are you talking about a defined group or about people in general? The majority of these residents is this survey; most residents is a claim about residents everywhere. And how exact do you need to be? In speech, a rounded fraction beats a decimal every time: roughly three quarters is easier to hold in the head than 77.5 per cent.

Patterns worth learning whole
  • the majority of / the vast majority of — over half, and clearly over half.
  • one in three / one in ten — a proportion, always with a singular verb: one in ten owns a boat.
  • a significant number of — enough to matter, without saying how many.
  • a handful of — a very small number, and slightly informal.
  • account for — Retired residents account for a third of the total.
  • a sharp rise in / a steady decline in — the noun phrase for a change over time.
  • twice as many… as — the commonest comparison, and the one most often got wrong.

11 · Read this before the extra practice.
Describing figures without reading them out

A reader does not want the numbers; they want the shape. English has a ladder of phrases for that, and each rung is a claim you can defend from the data: all of / nearly all of / the vast majority of → the majority of / most of / well over half of → half of / roughly half of / one in two → a significant number of / roughly a third of / one in three → a small number of / one in ten / only a few of → hardly any of / almost none of / a handful of.

Two grammatical points travel with them. First, of the appears whenever you mean this particular group: most of the residents we asked, not most of residents. Second, the verb agrees with the noun after of: a third of the members are retired, but a third of the budget is spent on rent.

Movement, and how much to claim

Change up: a sharp rise in, steady growth in, a slight increase in. Change down: a sharp fall in, a slight drop in, a steady decline in. The pattern is adjective + noun + in, and the verb version follows the same scale: numbers rose sharply / fell slightly / declined steadily.

Hedging is part of the grammar here, not decoration. Roughly, around, just over, just under, nearly, approximately let you make a claim the figures actually support: just over half is honest where most would be a stretch. The safest habit at B2 is to name the base as well as the proportion: of the 340 residents we asked, roughly a third…

Errors to watch: the most of residents → most of the residents · a third of the members is retired → are retired · the numbers raised sharply → rose sharply · a sharp rise of complaints → a sharp rise in complaints.

4 · Read the model.
Model · a report on the survey

Four hundred residents of the floating homes answered the survey in September, which is almost everybody on the five marinas.

The strongest result concerns the sharing of tools and labour: the vast majority said they borrow from a neighbour rather than buy, and roughly three quarters go to the September festival, which the residents decorate the dock for themselves. Exactly half have lived here for more than ten years, and the majority still work in the city, so this is neither a retirement community nor a commuter suburb but something between the two.

Twice as many residents share tools as own a second vehicle. Hardly any — fewer than one in twenty — would move back across the bay, and only a handful own a property elsewhere. Against that, there has been a sharp rise in prices in the last decade and steady growth in the number of new arrivals who work in technology.

What the figures do not show is what happens when the two groups need different things from the same dock. That question is for the next meeting.
